findings.title: Cookie-authed multipart uploads have no CSRF defense
findings.principle: Every route that accepts multipart/form-data and authenticates via the Supabase session cookie (createServerSupabaseClient() + auth.getUser()) must add an explicit CSRF defense before shipping: either require a custom header a plain HTML form cannot send (e.g. verify Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin, or a double-submit token), or switch the route to the same manually-attached Authorization: Bearer pattern app/api/salons/[slug]/gallery/route.ts already uses. A route is exempt from this rule ONLY if it is strictly JSON (Content-Type: application/json) or bearer-token-authenticated; the combination of multipart/form-data plus cookie auth is never exempt, no matter how small the surface looks.
findings.why: A cookie is attached automatically by the browser on a simple cross-site <form> POST (SameSite=Lax permits it on a top-level navigation), and multipart/form-data is a CORS-simple content type, so no preflight ever fires and the origin allowlist in middleware.ts is never consulted. An attacker's page can therefore silently trigger the write while the victim is merely logged into Solen in the same browser. This directly falsifies the project's own stated CSRF safety argument for exactly the routes that use this shape: security.md section 4 builds its whole 'Solen has no real CSRF surface' conclusion on every mutating route being JSON + CORS-allowlisted, and explicitly names multipart/form-data as the one shape that would silently defeat it -- treating that as a hypothetical future risk rather than checking whether it already exists.
findings.local_evidence: 8 of the 9 app/api/**/route.ts files calling req.formData() authenticate via createServerSupabaseClient()+auth.getUser() (cookie-based, no header the browser wouldn't auto-send): app/api/clients/[id]/photos/route.ts:13-14, app/api/salon/documents/route.ts:9-10, app/api/profile/avatar/route.ts:38-39, app/api/services/[id]/photos/route.ts:14-15, app/api/reviews/[id]/photos/route.ts:14-15, app/api/dashboard/coiffeur/formula-photo/route.ts:13-14, app/api/admin/discovery/upload/route.ts:11-12, app/api/services/import/route.ts:10-11. Only app/api/salons/[slug]/gallery/route.ts:57 reads an Authorization: Bearer header a form cannot forge, and is therefore CSRF-safe by construction; the other 8 are not. Practical impact per route: forced upload of an attacker-chosen (but MIME-allowlisted) image onto a client's before/after photo record, a salon's verification document, a user's profile avatar, or a review's photo gallery, with the victim never seeing it happen.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rl "\.formData()" app/api --include=route.ts -> 9 files, individually checked for auth mechanism. grep -rn "csrf|CSRF|X-CSRF|double-submit|Sec-Fetch-Site" app lib .claude/hooks _rules _backend-system -> 0 hits anywhere in code, hooks, or docs; no CSRF token/header concept exists at all in this codebase.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: _backend-system/research/security.md section 4 correctly derives that JSON+CORS-allowlist protects Solen's JSON routes from CSRF, and explicitly names multipart/form-data as the one shape that would silently defeat that protection ('if a future route ever accepts multipart/form-data... this protection silently stops applying to that one route and nobody will notice until it's exploited'). It frames this as a future risk to watch for, not a present fact; it did not check whether any route already has this shape. _rules/SECURITY_RULES.md has no CSRF rule at all (S1-S6 cover auth/RLS/validation/secrets, none mention CSRF or form-based auth).
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md (once written), security section, as a named row; a new Rule in _rules/SECURITY_RULES.md; a shared helper (e.g. requireAuthWithFormCsrfCheck()) used by the 8 affected routes.
findings.enforcement: gate: a grep-based PreToolUse check flagging any new/edited route.ts that combines req.formData() with createServerSupabaseClient()/auth.getUser() and no same-origin/custom-header check, mirroring the project's existing no-getsession-authz-gate.py pattern (advisory, since full taint analysis is out of reach for a grep gate).

findings.title: Every upload route trusts client file.type; zero server-side magic-byte checks exist
findings.principle: Every route that accepts a file upload verifies the file's real type by reading its first bytes and checking the format's magic-byte signature server-side (e.g. via the file-type package or an equivalent manual check), in addition to, never instead of, the client-declared file.type/extension allowlist, before the bytes are written to Storage or used to set the object's served Content-Type.
findings.why: file.type is a string the client's browser (or a hand-crafted multipart request) sets on the File object; OWASP's File Upload Cheat Sheet is explicit that it 'cannot be trusted, as it is trivial to spoof.' Solen already had one real incident from trusting it: service-photos let an unchecked file.type become the object's served Content-Type on a public bucket, hosting arbitrary HTML/SVG from a trusted *.supabase.co domain. That fix closed the gap at the Storage-layer bucket config for that one bucket; the application-layer root cause (trusting file.type at all) is untouched and repeats identically in every other upload route today.
findings.local_evidence: Every one of the 5 checked image/document upload routes gates solely on file.type string membership plus file.size, with the storage extension derived independently and unsanitized from the client-supplied filename: app/api/clients/[id]/photos/route.ts:63 (type check), :76 (ext = file.name.split('.').pop()); app/api/services/[id]/photos/route.ts:44,59; app/api/reviews/[id]/photos/route.ts:53,60; app/api/salons/[slug]/gallery/route.ts:104,127; app/api/salon/documents/route.ts:50,54. None of the 5 read the file's own buffer bytes at any point before upload.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rln "file-type|fileTypeFromBuffer|magic.*byte|fileSignature" app lib -> 0 hits. grep -c "\"file-type\"" package.json -> 0 (the package is not a dependency). grep for magic-byte anywhere in _backend-system/_rules -> only appears as an OWASP citation in research/security.md section 14 and research/file-storage.md section 7, both explicitly marked Unverified ('a route-by-route pass against that checklist was not done this run').
findings.existing_coverage: partial: security.md section 14 and file-storage.md section 7 both correctly name magic-byte validation as the missing OWASP control and both leave the actual per-route state as Unverified. This research resolves that Unverified item directly: the gap is real, confirmed, and codebase-wide across every image/document upload route, not a hypothetical.
findings.where_it_should_live: LAW.md file-storage/security section; a single shared lib/uploads/validateFileSignature.ts helper imported by every upload route (one place to fix, five call sites to update).
findings.enforcement: gate: an advisory PreToolUse reminder (same shape as ai-prompt-untrusted-guard.py) firing when a new/edited route reads formData().get(...) as File without importing the shared signature-check helper.

findings.title: Unescaped salon name in breadcrumb JSON-LD is a live stored-XSS vector
findings.principle: Every dangerouslySetInnerHTML call that embeds JSON.stringify() of an object containing any DB-sourced or user-editable field goes through one shared, tested helper (e.g. safeJsonLdStringify()) that escapes '<' so a value containing '</script>' cannot terminate the script tag early. Raw JSON.stringify() is never passed directly into dangerouslySetInnerHTML anywhere in the codebase, including call sites whose data is 'currently' static, since a later edit can silently make it dynamic.
findings.why: JSON.stringify does not escape forward slashes, so a literal '</script>' inside a string value survives verbatim into the HTML source. The browser's HTML parser runs before JS parsing and closes the <script> tag on that literal text regardless of JS-string-escaping rules, letting anything that follows execute as raw markup -- the exact backend-caused XSS pattern OWASP's XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet names for JSON-LD-in-script blocks. This is not theoretical here: the fix already exists in this codebase, applied inconsistently.
findings.local_evidence: app/[locale]/salon/[slug]/layout.tsx:128-138 builds a BreadcrumbList schema whose final item is { name: salon?.name ?? slug } -- salon.name is read straight from the salons table and is editable by the salon owner via the dashboard -- and renders it with dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: JSON.stringify(breadcrumb) }}, with zero escaping. The same page, one file over, app/[locale]/_components/salon/SalonDetailV3.tsx:177-182, DOES escape '<' before stringifying its own JSON-LD block, with an explicit code comment naming the '</script>' breakout it defends against ('a salon name containing "</script>" can't break out of the script tag'). The correct fix exists in the repo; it was simply never applied to the sibling call site rendering the identical field on the identical page.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn "safeJsonLd|jsonLdSafe|escapeJsonLd" lib app -> 0 hits (no shared/exported helper exists; the one working escape is an inline, unexported .replace() inside SalonDetailV3.tsx). grep -rl dangerouslySetInnerHTML app -> 7 files; the other 5 (nails/spa/coiffeur/barbershop/partner pages) call JSON.stringify(breadcrumb)/JSON.stringify(faq)/JSON.stringify(jsonLd) directly with no escaping at all -- currently benign because their content is static category FAQ copy, not DB data, but nothing structural prevents the next edit from feeding one of them a DB field the way layout.tsx does.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: _backend-system/research/security.md section 3 named this exact class as 'the single highest-value follow-up from this section' and explicitly left it Unverified ('whether the dangerouslySetInnerHTML call sites... ever include unescaped salon-supplied free-text... not verified this pass'). This research resolves the Unverified item: one call site is safe, its sibling rendering the same field on the same page is not.
findings.where_it_should_live: a shared helper in lib/seo.ts (or a new lib/seo/jsonld.ts), used by all 7 call sites; LAW.md security/XSS section.
findings.enforcement: gate: a grep-based PreToolUse check flagging dangerouslySetInnerHTML paired with a raw JSON.stringify( call not routed through the shared helper.

findings.title: The SSRF guard protects one call site out of at least six that fetch non-hardcoded URLs
findings.principle: Every server-side fetch() whose URL argument is not a compile-time string literal pointing at a fixed, hardcoded first-party or well-known vendor host is passed through assertSafeFetchUrl() (or an equivalent IP-range check) before the request fires, with no exception carved out for 'the URL came from our own database' or 'the URL came from a trusted third-party API's own response' -- both are still request-time data, not compile-time constants, and both have been the actual origin of a URL that reached the guarded code path in this codebase.
findings.why: The guard was built after a real incident: lib/ai-vision.ts fetched an attacker-supplied image_url with zero guard, letting a prod server reach cloud metadata or scan internal ports. Wiring the fix onto only the one route that caused the incident, while structurally identical fetches of non-hardcoded URLs exist elsewhere untouched, means the vulnerability CLASS was never actually closed -- only its first known instance was patched. The next incident is a certainty on the current trajectory, not a hypothetical risk.
findings.local_evidence: assertSafeFetchUrl is imported by exactly one caller in the entire codebase: lib/ai-vision.ts (plus the guard's own definition file, lib/security/ssrf-guard.ts). Meanwhile at least 4 other routes fetch a URL that is neither a literal nor already range-checked: app/api/discovery/thumb/[id]/route.ts:160 fetch(freshUrl), where freshUrl is a field from a TikTok oEmbed API response; app/api/admin/discovery/staging/route.ts:81 fetch(item.image_url), where image_url is a DB column populated by an import/ingest pipeline; app/api/admin/discovery/backfill/route.ts:131 fetch(imageUrl, ...); app/api/admin/nail/generate/route.ts:108 fetch(imageUrl), fetching back a URL from a third-party (fal.ai) generation response.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rln assertSafeFetchUrl app lib -> lib/ai-vision.ts and the guard's own file only. Checked .claude/hooks and ~/.claude/hooks for any fetch/SSRF-related PreToolUse gate: none exists beyond the guard's own source file; nothing requires a new fetch() call with a variable URL to route through it.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: _backend-system/research/security.md section 5 documents the guard's own implementation thoroughly and correctly, including its one known internal gap (DNS rebinding), but frames the finding as 'Solen fit... implements the IP-range-blocklist half of this correctly and thoroughly' -- verifying the guard's code quality, not whether it is actually reached by every route that needs it. Call-site coverage was never audited.
findings.where_it_should_live: LAW.md security/SSRF section, naming the specific fetch call sites above; the guard is already the right shape, this is a wiring gap, not a design gap.
findings.enforcement: gate: a PreToolUse/grep check flagging a new or edited await fetch(<non-literal>) in app/** or lib/** with no assertSafeFetchUrl call in the same file (advisory, the same shape as ai-prompt-untrusted-guard.py, since a hard block would need real taint analysis).

findings.title: CSP is still absent, so the one bug found above (finding 03) has zero backstop
findings.principle: Solen serves a Content-Security-Policy header (Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only for one full deploy cycle first, then enforcing Content-Security-Policy) with an explicit script-src/style-src/img-src/connect-src domain allowlist covering at minimum Stripe.js, Google Maps, PostHog, and 'self', before any further work proceeds on the assumption that a missed-escaping bug has a second line of defense.
findings.why: netlify.toml already carries every other OWASP-recommended header (nosniff, HSTS with preload, frame-ancestors via X-Frame-Options, a scoped Permissions-Policy) except CSP. Without it, a single missed-escape bug anywhere in the app -- finding input-abuse-03 above is a concrete, currently-live example -- has no second line of defense; CSP is specifically the control that would still have contained that exact class of bug even after a code review missed the escaping.
findings.local_evidence: grep -n "Content-Security-Policy" netlify.toml returns zero lines; the [[headers]] block for "/*" defines exactly 6 header keys (X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, X-DNS-Prefetch-Control, Permissions-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security), none of them CSP.
findings.absence_proof: grep across _backend-system, _rules, .claude/hooks, and netlify.toml for Content-Security-Policy -> the string only appears as research prose/citations inside _backend-system/research/security.md section 6; it never appears as an actual deployed header, a tracked TODO, or a LAW.md row (LAW.md does not exist).
findings.existing_coverage: full analysis already exists and is high quality: security.md section 6 names this 'the single highest-value gap this file found,' gives a concrete rollout plan (report-only first, explicit allowlist before nonces), and even flags the SSL-config-generator URL migration as a volatile fact worth recording. Zero of that analysis has been implemented. This is a pure research-written-but-never-shipped gap, not a research gap.
findings.where_it_should_live: netlify.toml; LAW.md as a tracked, dated row so a future session sees it was already decided and just needs shipping.
findings.enforcement: checklist item today; once shipped, a deploy-time smoke check that greps the live response headers for the CSP key would keep it from silently regressing (a config typo dropping the whole [[headers]] block is explicitly named as a known Netlify trap in security.md's own Myths section).

findings.title: AI prompt-injection wrapping is adopted in under half the LLM call sites and is enforced only as a same-session reminder
findings.principle: Every LLM prompt built from a field whose value traces back outside Solen's own server-authored strings (a request body, a DB column a user or an external ingest pipeline populated, DOM text captured by a visual editor, uploaded content) is wrapped with wrapUntrustedInput() before being concatenated into the prompt. A file that calls an LLM without using it must carry an explicit code comment stating why every input is a compile-time constant, so the omission reads as a decision, not a miss.
findings.why: This is not hypothetical: the project's own hook docstring records a prior real incident (the 'Part-D audit,' customer text spliced raw into a Gemini prompt) that is exactly this failure class. A reminder-only PreToolUse hook that only fires when a session touches the file cannot retroactively protect code that shipped before the hook existed, or a call shape the hook's regex doesn't match, so partial adoption today means the exact same incident class is still reachable through the routes the hook never got to.
findings.local_evidence: Of 14 files calling generateContent/GoogleGenerativeAI, only 6 use wrapUntrustedInput: app/api/translate, app/api/salons/[slug]/ai-info, app/api/ai/recommend, app/api/ai/suggest-service, app/api/ai/intake-recommendation, app/api/services/suggest. app/api/discovery/generate-description/route.ts:46-53 builds a prompt directly from item.style_name/category/gender/texture/tags/vibe/occasion -- discovery_items fields that trace back to the TikTok import/auto-tagging pipeline, i.e. content that originated outside Solen's own trust boundary -- with zero wrapping.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rln wrapUntrustedInput app lib -> 8 files (6 routes + the helper definition + lib/editor-prompts.ts). grep -rln "generateContent|GoogleGenerativeAI" app lib -> 14 files. The unwrapped remainder: discovery/generate-description, admin/discovery/smart-import, admin/generate-roadmap, admin/discovery/check-ai, recommendations/route.ts (generative, all real gaps), plus lib/search/category-detect.ts and lib/search/embeddings.ts (embeddings calls, lower relevance, no free-text generation to hijack).
findings.existing_coverage: partial: .claude/hooks/ai-prompt-untrusted-guard.py exists and is confirmed wired into .claude/settings.json (3 hook registrations found), and is explicitly advisory by its own docstring ('a REMINDER, not a hard block'). It fires only on a Write/Edit touching the file in the CURRENT session; discovery/generate-description already existed before the hook was added (2026-07-14) and has not been revisited since.
findings.where_it_should_live: a one-time backfill sweep of the ~5 unwrapped generative files; LAW.md AI-safety section stating the wrap-everything rule explicitly (it currently lives only inside a hook's docstring and one lib file's header comment, not in any frozen law document).
findings.enforcement: the hook is already the enforcement mechanism for new/edited files going forward; the open gap is specifically pre-existing code the hook never got a chance to flag, which needs a manual sweep, not a new gate.

findings.title: 22% of mutating routes hand-roll body validation instead of using the shared zod schema path
findings.principle: Every route handler that calls req.json()/request.json() on a mutating (POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE) request validates the parsed body with validateBody(schema, body) from lib/validations.ts before reading any field. An inline check such as if (!code || typeof code !== 'string' || code.trim().length < 4) is not an acceptable substitute for a zod schema, because it has to be correctly re-derived by hand at every call site instead of being enforced once.
findings.why: The project's own Rule S4 already states 'ALWAYS validate request bodies with zod schemas' and 'NEVER trust req.json() without schema validation' as a should-be-mandatory rule. Nearly a quarter of mutating routes not following it means the rule is aspirational rather than actually true today, and every hand-rolled check is a fresh opportunity to miss a case a shared schema would catch for free -- a missing length cap, an unchecked nested field, an optional field the author forgot.
findings.local_evidence: 39 of 174 (22%) route.ts files calling req.json()/request.json() have neither safeParse nor validateBody anywhere in the file, including app/api/vouchers/validate/route.ts, app/api/vouchers/confirm/route.ts, app/api/favorites/toggle/route.ts, app/api/staff/[id]/route.ts, app/api/services/reorder/route.ts, app/api/dashboard/clients/[id]/notes/route.ts, app/api/dashboard/clients/[id]/tags/route.ts, and 32 others (full list captured this run). Spot-checked app/api/vouchers/validate/route.ts and app/api/coming-soon-notify/route.ts: both do careful, correct hand-rolled checks today, which is exactly why this is worth codifying now, before the pattern that happens to be careful today gets copy-pasted less carefully into route #40.
findings.absence_proof: comm -23 of (grep -rlE "req\.json\(\)|request\.json\(\)" app/api) vs (grep -rlE "safeParse|validateBody" app/api) across route.ts files -> 39 files. grep -rn "validateBody|zod" _rules/SECURITY_RULES.md -> Rule S4 states the requirement in prose only; none of the project's existing PreToolUse gates (checked .claude/hooks) verify a route actually calls validateBody.
findings.existing_coverage: the rule exists in _rules/SECURITY_RULES.md Rule S4/S5 as an ALWAYS/MANDATORY prose statement; it has no gate behind it, and the 22% figure shows the prose is not self-enforcing by convention either.
findings.where_it_should_live: a new PreToolUse gate alongside the existing no-getsession-authz-gate.py; _rules/SECURITY_RULES.md Rule S4 gets a cross-reference to the gate once it exists.
findings.enforcement: gate: require-body-schema-gate.py -- flags a new/edited route calling req.json() on a mutating verb with no validateBody/safeParse call in the same file.

findings.title: The enumeration-oracle defense pattern is correct everywhere but exists only as five independently-repeated code comments, never a named rule
findings.principle: Any endpoint that looks up a resource by a client-supplied code or token and is reachable without authentication must: (a) use exact-match comparison, never .ilike/.like; (b) return one identical generic message/status for every failure branch (not found, expired, already redeemed, wrong owner); and (c) sit behind a tight IP-keyed rate limiter sized to the token's entropy. This is written once, in one place, so the next such endpoint inherits it by reading a rule rather than an author re-deriving it from first principles or copy-pasting a sibling route's comment.
findings.why: The pattern is currently correct everywhere it appears in this codebase, which is exactly the situation where writing the rule down is cheapest and most valuable -- there is no fix to argue for, only a codification. Solen's product surface (gift vouchers, loyalty QR codes, walk-in tokens, referral codes) is structurally code/token-heavy and will keep adding these endpoints; a pattern that is correct only because each author happened to remember it is fragile in a way a named rule is not.
findings.local_evidence: the identical generic-message pattern, each with its own independently-written explanatory comment re-deriving the same reasoning, appears in app/api/referral/validate/route.ts, app/api/referral/complete/route.ts, app/api/bookings/guest-lookup/route.ts, app/api/search/event/route.ts, and app/api/vouchers/validate/route.ts:12 (GENERIC_INVALID_MESSAGE, with a comment naming the exact oracle it closes: 'an attacker could tell code doesn't exist apart from code exists but is unpaid/redeemed/expired').
findings.absence_proof: grep -riE enumerat across _backend-system, _rules, _design-system, CLAUDE.md -> the concept is discussed from three different angles in three different research files (rate-limiting.md section 3 covers the rate-limit angle, data-modeling.md covers the UUID-choice angle, authn.md covers the password-reset angle), but none of them, nor any _rules file, states the single general endpoint-shape rule above as one named row a route author would find by searching once.
findings.existing_coverage: partial and scattered across three unconnected research files by three different framings; no single cross-cutting rule exists in _rules/SECURITY_RULES.md or anywhere else.
findings.where_it_should_live: _rules/SECURITY_RULES.md as a new Rule S7 ('public lookup-by-code endpoints'), cross-referenced from LAW.md once it exists.
findings.enforcement: checklist / behavioral rule -- verifying 'every failure branch returns the identical message' is not reliably gate-able by grep, so a code-review checklist item is the realistic enforcement here.
